AI Has a Power Problem: Why the U.S. Power Grid Can't Keep Up | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 69

Kallo describes power, grid equipment and skilled labor as bottlenecks to AI construction and favors GE Vernova's long order cycle. He discusses Tesla autonomy and storage, predicts a potential SpaceX-Tesla combination, and explains tariff-driven solar uncertainty. Eisman owns GE Vernova, questions Tesla's valuation and autonomy promises, and adopts the power-and-labor constraint thesis without endorsing all guest forecasts.

Source version, speaker attribution and transcript cautions

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

YouTube automatic captions; speaker attribution requires context

Ben Kallo is the interviewed Baird analyst. Eisman asks questions, discloses GE Vernova ownership and closes with an explicit distinction between Kallo's bullish Tesla thesis and his own skepticism.

  • Severe unit issues: captions give US capacity as 150 GW, reverse MW/GW conversion, and call the 30 GW annual estimate 30 MW in Eisman's closing summary. Audio confirmation is required before assigning these numerical errors to either speaker.
  • SMR first-unit timing is described as 2035, while OPG's published plan is 2030; distinguish analyst delay forecast from official schedule.
  • The closing summary says the guest likes no solar names, but Kallo explicitly says he recommends Nextpower.

How he reasons here

  • Distinguish announced projects from funded, interconnected construction and avoid double counting.
  • Identify speed-to-power and firm capacity rather than nominal generating capacity alone.
  • Value long-cycle equipment with backlog, service revenue and delivery timing.
  • Separate an EV business valuation from autonomy and robotics optionality.
